agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: First-class and stated at several levels. The whole product is a CLI (init, ingest, inbox import, compile, query, tasks, retrieval, explore, lint, watch, mcp, graph serve), installable globally from npm, and the vault can be exposed directly over MCP for compatible clients. Vault-aware rules can be installed into a coding agent with one command, and task ledgers record what an agent did. Because every artifact is a local file the CLI writes and the viewer reads, an agent can also consume the graph and wiki directly from disk without any API at all.

hlido_opinion.headline: Builds a durable local knowledge graph with provenance instead of an ephemeral retrieval index - and says its screenshot is the real installed app, not a mock.
hlido_opinion.body: The distinction this product leads with is the right one. Ordinary retrieval augmentation produces a disposable index: you embed some documents, query them, and the artifact has no independent value. SwarmVault's claim is that it compiles a persistent knowledge artifact that gets richer as sources are added - raw sources, a Markdown wiki and graph state, all as local files you can open and inspect. Immutable source manifests with content hashes, provenance tracking on graph edges and auto-generated wiki pages are the mechanisms named, and a schema file per vault sets naming rules, categories and grounding expectations so compile and query behaviour is governed rather than emergent. Two choices stand out. The first is that it works with no API key at all via a built-in heuristic workflow, with model providers optional for richer synthesis - so the tool is usable before any spending decision. The second is an unusual piece of honesty: the surface states that the viewer screenshot comes from the installed package running in a real browser rather than a design mock, and that the viewer reads the same local files the CLI writes. Vendors almost never volunteer that distinction, and the fact that someone chose to is consistent with the anti-drift linting feature, which detects stale sources, conflicting claims, missing citations and coverage gaps. The surface also offers four named worked examples rather than abstract feature claims. What is absent is any public operating history, any statement of scale limits for the graph, and - captured on the day - a clear primary call to action or pricing statement.

tier_rationale: STEADY (75) because the central distinction from ordinary retrieval is architectural and visible (durable local files, immutable hashed source manifests, provenance on the graph, a per-vault schema governing behaviour), the tool is genuinely usable with no API key before any spend, the agent surface is first-class (CLI plus MCP plus one-command agent rules), worked examples replace abstract claims, and the page volunteers that its screenshot is the real installed product rather than a mock. Not VITAL because no operating history, release cadence or maintainer commitment is visible, no scale or performance bound is stated for the graph as a vault grows, the anti-drift linting that would most distinguish it is described but not demonstrated, and the captured surface offered no clear primary action or access terms beyond the MIT licence.
what_it_does_well: Produces a durable, inspectable artifact - raw sources, a Markdown wiki and graph state as local files - rather than a disposable retrieval index
Creates immutable source manifests with content hashes and tracks provenance through the graph
Governs compile and query behaviour with a per-vault schema file setting naming rules, categories and grounding expectations
Works fully offline with a built-in heuristic workflow and no API keys, making model providers an optional upgrade rather than a precondition
States that the viewer screenshot is the installed package in a real browser, not a design mock, and that the viewer reads the same files the CLI writes
Includes anti-drift linting aimed at stale sources, conflicting claims, missing citations and coverage gaps - the failure modes a growing knowledge base actually has
Offers four concrete worked examples (code repo, research capture, review loop, book reading) instead of abstract feature lists
Stages compile changes through approval bundles and candidate promotion rather than silent rewrites
what_it_fails_at: No public operating history, release cadence or maintainer commitment
No scale or performance bound stated for the graph as a vault grows - the question any serious user asks second
The anti-drift linting that most distinguishes it is described but never demonstrated on the surface
No clear primary call to action was present on the captured surface, which split the reader across several install paths
Access terms beyond the MIT licence are unstated - no pricing, support or hosted option described
Positioned as part of a wider network whose relationship to this project's continuity is not explained
best_for: Teams that want an auditable, versionable knowledge artifact in their repository rather than a vendor-hosted index
Researchers accumulating sources over months who need provenance and citation tracking to hold up later
Operators who need to start fully offline with no API key and decide about model spend afterwards
Developers wanting a knowledge base their coding agent can query over MCP and that lives beside the code
not_recommended_for: Teams wanting a managed hosted service - this is a local-first CLI and desktop app you run yourself
Anyone needing a supported product with a maintenance commitment, since none is published
Use cases with very large corpora, where the absence of any stated scale bound is a real risk
Buyers who need pricing and support terms before adopting a knowledge system
red_flags: No operating history or maintenance commitment for a tool whose entire value proposition is that the artifact compounds over months and years
No stated scale limit, so the growth the product is designed around is exactly the condition whose behaviour is unspecified

compared_to.verdict_diff: LlamaIndex is a mature framework for building retrieval over your data, with far more integrations and an operating record; SwarmVault is a packaged local-first product whose output is a durable inspectable wiki and graph rather than an index you embed in an application. Choose LlamaIndex to build; choose SwarmVault to accumulate a knowledge artifact you can read.

Letta focuses on persistent agent memory inside an agent runtime; SwarmVault focuses on a human- and agent-readable knowledge graph compiled from sources with provenance. Choose Letta for memory inside a running agent; choose SwarmVault when the knowledge itself is the deliverable.
